units.title: Greetings & politeness basics
units.intro:
Daily life in Japan runs on a small set of fixed phrases. You will hear the same greetings, thanks and apologies dozens of times a day, and using them smoothly matters more than perfect grammar.

The most important choice is **politeness level**. With strangers, shop staff, neighbors, officials and colleagues, speak in the polite {です／ます} style. Casual speech is for friends, family and people who have clearly invited you to relax. If you are unsure, stay polite: nobody is offended by politeness, but sudden casual speech can sound rude.

Greetings usually come with a small bow ({お辞儀[じぎ]}). For everyday situations, a slight nod of the head is enough; deeper bows are for apologies, formal thanks and ceremonies. You do not need to bow and shake hands at the same time, though many Japanese people will offer a handshake to foreigners.

When you enter a shop, staff will call out {いらっしゃいませ} (welcome). You are not expected to answer; a nod or simply carrying on is normal.

One word does a lot of work: {すみません}. It means excuse me (to get attention), sorry (for a small mistake), and even thank you (when someone has gone to trouble for you). Learn it first.

Finally, names: add {さん} to other people's names, but never to your own.

phrases.jp: おはようございます。
phrases.en: Good morning.
phrases.note: Polite form. Among friends, just {おはよう}. Some workplaces use it as the first greeting of a shift, whatever the time.

phrases.jp: こんにちは。
phrases.en: Hello. / Good afternoon.
phrases.note: Used from late morning to early evening. Not normally used with your own colleagues or family.

phrases.jp: こんばんは。
phrases.en: Good evening.

phrases.jp: ありがとうございます。
phrases.en: Thank you.

phrases.jp: どうもありがとうございました。
phrases.en: Thank you very much (for what you did).
phrases.note: The past form {ございました} thanks someone for something already finished, such as at the end of a shop visit.

phrases.jp: すみません。
phrases.en: Excuse me. / Sorry. / Thanks (for your trouble).

phrases.jp: ごめんなさい。
phrases.en: I'm sorry.
phrases.note: A personal apology, softer and less formal. In business, use {申[もう]し訳[わけ]ありません} instead.

phrases.jp: お願[ねが]いします。
phrases.en: Please. (when asking for something)
phrases.note: Put it after a noun to request it: {これ、お願[ねが]いします} (This one, please).

phrases.en: I'm fine. / No thanks, I'm OK.
phrases.note: Very common as a polite refusal, e.g. when offered a bag. Context decides whether it means yes or no.

phrases.en: Is English OK (for you)?

phrases.en: Excuse me (as I enter / leave).
phrases.note: Said when entering a room, leaving, or passing in front of someone.

phrases.en: (before eating) / Thank you for the meal. (after eating)

phrases.en: See you. (casual)

{お元気[げんき]ですか} is not an everyday how are you. It is used when you haven't seen someone for a while. Day to day, people comment on the weather instead.
A direct {いいえ} (no) can feel blunt. People soften refusals with {ちょっと…} or {大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]です}.
Bow while saying the phrase, not after it, and keep your eyes down slightly. Do not overthink it; a sincere small bow is always fine.
Never add {さん} to your own name or your family members' names when talking to others.

units.title: Self-introduction
units.intro:
You will introduce yourself constantly in your first months: to neighbors, at language exchanges, in a share house, at the ward office and later at work. In Japan this is called {自己紹介[じこしょうかい]}, and it follows a fairly fixed pattern, which makes it easy to prepare.

A typical self-introduction has four or five parts:

- An opener: {はじめまして} (nice to meet you, used only at a first meeting).
- Your name: {〜です}, or the more formal {〜と申[もう]します}.
- Where you are from and/or where you live now.
- What you do (job, study) and perhaps a hobby.
- A closing: {よろしくお願[ねが]いします}, which roughly means I look forward to our relationship, please treat me well.

Keep it short. Japanese self-introductions are usually brief and modest; ten to twenty seconds is perfectly normal in a casual setting. Bow slightly at the end with {よろしくお願[ねが]いします}.

Foreign names are written in katakana. Decide early how you want to be called, and say it clearly. In formal settings Japanese people use family names, so colleagues may call you by your family name plus {さん}. If you prefer your first name, it is fine to say so: {〜と呼[よ]んでください}.

Expect a few standard follow-up questions: where you are from, how long you have been in Japan, and whether you like Japanese food.

{はじめまして} is only for the very first meeting. Next time, use a normal greeting.
Avoid long personal stories in a first introduction. Modesty is valued; let people ask follow-up questions.
At work, introductions become more formal and are often followed by an exchange of business cards. See the office units later in this track.

units.title: Numbers, money & shopping
units.intro:
Japan's currency is the yen ({円[えん]}). Coins come in 1, 5, 10, 50, 100 and 500 yen; common notes are 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000 yen (a 2,000-yen note exists but is rare). New banknote designs were introduced in 2024, and older notes remain valid.

Japanese counts large numbers in units of ten thousand ({万[まん]}), not thousands. So 10,000 is {一万[いちまん]}, 50,000 is {五万[ごまん]}, and 120,000 is {十二万[じゅうにまん]}. Rents and salaries are almost always quoted this way, so practice it until it is automatic.

Prices shown to consumers must include consumption tax, so the big number on the tag is usually what you pay ({税込[ぜいこみ]}). You may also see the pre-tax price ({税抜[ぜいぬき]}) in smaller print. Food bought to take away is taxed at a lower rate than eating in.

Cash is still widely used, but card, IC-card and QR-code payments are now common in cities. Smaller shops and restaurants may still be cash only, so keep some cash on you.

At the register, put your money in the small tray rather than handing it directly to the cashier, and receive your change the same way or by hand. Plastic shopping bags cost a few yen, so you will be asked if you need one. Note that tax-free shopping is for short-term visitors; once you live in Japan you are generally not eligible.

Shop staff speak very polite Japanese ({ございます}, {いただけます}). You only need to answer in normal {です／ます}.

units.title: Convenience stores & restaurants
units.intro:
Convenience stores ({コンビニ}) are a lifeline for new residents. Besides food and drinks, most let you pay utility bills and some tax bills with the payment slip, withdraw cash from an ATM that accepts many foreign cards, print and copy documents, send and receive parcels, and buy event tickets. They are open long hours, often 24/7.

At the register you will hear a few standard questions: whether to heat your lunch box ({温[あたた]めますか}), whether you need chopsticks or a spoon, whether you need a bag, and whether you have a point card. Short answers like {はい、お願[ねが]いします} or {大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]です} cover almost everything.

In restaurants, staff greet you with {いらっしゃいませ} and ask how many people are in your group ({何名様[なんめいさま]ですか}). Many casual places, especially ramen and set-meal shops, use a ticket machine ({食券[しょっけん]}): you buy a ticket at the entrance and hand it to staff. Water or tea is usually free and refilled. To call staff, raise your hand and say {すみません}, or press the call button on the table if there is one.

There is no tipping in Japan; leaving money behind may cause staff to chase after you. You normally pay at the register near the exit, not at the table. Indoor smoking is now restricted in most restaurants, though some small bars still allow it.

units.title: Trains, IC cards & asking directions
units.intro:
Trains and subways are the backbone of daily life in Japanese cities. The easiest way to ride is a rechargeable IC card such as Suica, PASMO or ICOCA. The major cards work on most trains, subways and buses in the big metropolitan areas and at many shops, and you can also put one on many smartphones. Tap the card on the gate when you enter and again when you leave; the fare is deducted automatically. Top it up ({チャージ}) with cash at station machines.

If you commute, you will probably buy a commuter pass ({定期券[ていきけん]}) for your regular route. Many employers pay commuting costs ({通勤[つうきん]手当[てあて]}), so ask before you buy.

Trains come in several types, and faster ones skip stations: {各駅停車[かくえきていしゃ]} (local, stops everywhere), {快速[かいそく]} (rapid), {急行[きゅうこう]} (express), and {特急[とっきゅう]} (limited express, which often needs an extra ticket). Always check that your train stops at your station.

Train etiquette: keep your voice low, do not take phone calls, let people off before getting on, and leave priority seats ({優先席[ゆうせんせき]}) for those who need them. Some lines have women-only cars during rush hours. Last trains ({終電[しゅうでん]}) leave around midnight.

If you get lost, ask station staff or go to a police box ({交番[こうばん]}); officers there give directions all the time.

units.title: Emergencies & disaster preparation
units.intro:
Memorize two numbers: **110** for the police ({警察[けいさつ]}) and **119** for fire and ambulance ({消防[しょうぼう]}・{救急[きゅうきゅう]}). Both work free from any phone. When you call 119, the first question is {火事[かじ]ですか、救急[きゅうきゅう]ですか} (fire or medical emergency?). Then you will be asked for the address, what happened, and your name and phone number. Many emergency centers can connect to an interpreter, so stay on the line even if your Japanese runs out.

If you are unsure whether something needs an ambulance, many areas run a medical advice line on **#7119**; check whether yours does.

Japan has frequent earthquakes, and also typhoons, heavy rain and floods. Phones sound an emergency earthquake alert ({緊急地震速報[きんきゅうじしんそくほう]}) seconds before strong shaking. Protect your head, get under a sturdy table, and stay away from windows and tall furniture. After the shaking stops, check for fire and be ready for aftershocks ({余震[よしん]}). Near the coast, a tsunami warning means move to high ground immediately.

Prepare now: find your local hazard map and evacuation sites on your city's website. An {避難場所[ひなんばしょ]} is an open place to escape to right away; an {避難所[ひなんじょ]} is a shelter, often a school, where people stay. Keep an emergency bag ({非常[ひじょう]持[も]ち出[だ]し袋[ぶくろ]}) and store water and food for at least several days. After a big disaster, the **171** message dial lets families leave voice messages for each other.

Look up your area's hazard map and walk to your nearest evacuation site once, so you know the way.
Keep drinking water, non-perishable food, a flashlight, a battery pack, medicine, copies of documents and some cash ready at home.
Your embassy may offer a registration service for residents so it can contact you in a crisis; it is worth signing up.
Many local governments and the national tourism authority provide multilingual disaster information and apps. Install one and turn on notifications.

units.title: The doctor & pharmacy
units.intro:
For everyday illness, go to a local clinic ({クリニック} or {医院[いいん]}) rather than a big hospital. Clinics are organized by specialty: {内科[ないか]} (internal medicine, for colds, fever and stomach trouble), {耳鼻科[じびか]} (ear, nose and throat), {皮膚科[ひふか]} (skin), {整形外科[せいけいげか]} (bones, joints and injuries), {歯科[しか]} (dentist). Large hospitals often expect a referral letter ({紹介状[しょうかいじょう]}) and may charge an extra fee without one.

Bring proof of health insurance. Japan has been moving health insurance onto the My Number card, so many clinics now have a card reader at reception; if you have a different insurance document, bring that. With public insurance, most working-age adults pay a share of the cost (commonly 30%) at the counter. Some small clinics still accept only cash.

On your first visit ({初診[しょしん]}) you will fill in a questionnaire ({問診票[もんしんひょう]}) about your symptoms, allergies and current medication. Ask for an English version if there is one, or prepare your answers in advance with a translation app.

The doctor gives you a prescription ({処方箋[しょほうせん]}), which you take to a pharmacy ({薬局[やっきょく]}), often right next to the clinic. The pharmacist explains how to take the medicine and may offer a medication notebook ({お薬[くすり]手帳[てちょう]}) that records your prescriptions. Over-the-counter medicine is sold at drugstores. Note that some medicines common abroad are restricted in Japan; check official guidance before bringing medicine with you.

Write down your symptoms, when they started and any allergies in Japanese before you go. Showing a note is perfectly acceptable.
Keep receipts for medical costs. If your household's medical spending is high in a year, you may be able to claim a tax deduction.

units.title: Arrival: the airport & your residence card
units.intro:
If you enter Japan to live there for the mid to long term (for work, study, as a spouse and so on), immigration will check your passport and your visa or Certificate of Eligibility. At the major international airports, such as Narita, Haneda, Kansai and Chubu, you are usually handed your residence card ({在留[ざいりゅう]カード}) on the spot. If you arrive elsewhere, your passport is stamped and the card is sent to you after you register your address.

The residence card is your main ID in Japan. Adults are required to carry it at all times, and you will need it for almost every procedure: the ward office, bank, phone, apartment and job. Check it carefully as soon as you receive it. It shows your status of residence ({在留[ざいりゅう]資格[しかく]}), your period of stay ({在留[ざいりゅう]期間[きかん]}), and whether you are allowed to work.

After you find a place to live, you must register your address at the municipal office within 14 days (see the next unit).

To extend your stay, you apply to a regional immigration office before your period of stay ends; applications can generally be made from a few months before expiry. Requirements change, so always confirm the current rules with the Immigration Services Agency ({出入国[しゅつにゅうこく]在留[ざいりゅう]管理庁[かんりちょう]}). If you plan to leave Japan temporarily and come back, check the re-entry rules before you travel.

Practical tip: airports have counters where you can send heavy luggage to your new address by courier, so you can travel into the city light.

Check the work permission line on the card. If it is restricted, do not take on work outside what your status allows.
Keep digital copies of your passport, residence card and visa documents somewhere safe.
Immigration offices can be crowded. Many procedures can now be started online; check the Immigration Services Agency website first.
When you report a change, such as a new employer or a lost card, there are usually strict deadlines. Look them up the moment something changes.

units.title: The ward office: registration, My Number, insurance & pension
units.intro:
Your city or ward office ({市役所[しやくしょ]} or {区役所[くやくしょ]}) is where you become an official resident. Within 14 days of moving in, go there with your residence card and passport and file a moving-in notification ({転入届[てんにゅうとどけ]}). Staff will print your address on the back of your residence card. You can usually handle several things in the same visit:

- **Resident registration**. Once registered, you can request a certificate of residence ({住民票[じゅうみんひょう]}), which banks, employers and others often ask for.
- **My Number**. Every resident is assigned a 12-digit personal number used for tax, social security and other administration. A notification is mailed to your registered address, and you can apply for a My Number card, a photo ID that also works as a health insurance card and lets you get some certificates at convenience stores.
- **Health insurance**. If your employer enrolls you in its health insurance ({社会保険[しゃかいほけん]}), you use that. Otherwise you join National Health Insurance ({国民健康保険[こくみんけんこうほけん]}) at the office.
- **Pension**. Residents aged 20 to 59 are generally part of the public pension system: through the employee pension if you work for a company, or the national pension ({国民年金[こくみんねんきん]}) otherwise.

Rules, fees and required documents differ by municipality and change over time, so check your city's website (many have English pages) or ask at the counter. If you move again, file a moving-out notification ({転出届[てんしゅつとどけ]}) at your old office first, and do the same when you leave Japan.

If you cannot afford National Health Insurance or pension payments, ask about reductions or exemptions rather than just not paying. Unpaid amounts can cause problems later, including at visa renewal.
Bring a Japanese-speaking friend or use a translation app for your first visit. Many offices also have multilingual consultation services.

units.title: Bank account & phone contract
units.intro:
A bank account and a phone number are the next two things you need, and each tends to ask for the other. Many newcomers solve this by getting a data SIM or eSIM first, or by using a number arranged through their workplace or school.

**Banks.** You will need your residence card (with your registered address), a Japanese phone number, and sometimes proof of employment or study. Some banks also ask for a personal seal ({印鑑[いんかん]}), though many now accept a signature. Some banks are stricter with people who have only just arrived, so ask before you go. Japan Post Bank ({ゆうちょ銀行[ぎんこう]}) is a common first choice because it has branches and ATMs almost everywhere. Expect to be asked why you are opening the account; this is a routine anti-fraud check. Your cash card is usually sent to your registered address by registered mail, which is not forwarded.

Your salary will be paid by bank transfer ({振込[ふりこみ]}), and many bills can be paid by automatic debit ({口座[こうざ]振替[ふりかえ]}).

**Phones.** There are a few large carriers, their cheaper sub-brands, and many low-cost providers ({格安[かくやす]SIM}). Bring your residence card and a payment method; some providers require a credit card. Early cancellation penalties are much smaller than they once were, but always ask.

Important: never sell, lend or hand over your bank account or SIM to anyone, even when you leave Japan. This is a crime, and such accounts are used for fraud. Close them properly before you go.

units.title: Finding an apartment
units.intro:
Most rentals go through a real-estate agency ({不動産屋[ふどうさんや]}). You browse listings online or in the shop, arrange a viewing ({内見[ないけん]}), apply, pass a screening ({審査[しんさ]}) and then sign the contract.

The upfront costs surprise many newcomers. Typical items include:

- {敷金[しききん]}: a deposit, used for cleaning and repairs when you move out; the rest is returned.
- {礼金[れいきん]}: key money, a non-refundable payment to the landlord. Many listings now have none.
- {仲介[ちゅうかい]手数料[てすうりょう]}: the agency's fee.
- The first month's rent, fire insurance, a lock change fee and a guarantor company fee.

Together these often add up to several months' rent, so budget carefully and ask for a full estimate.

Landlords usually want a guarantor ({保証人[ほしょうにん]}). Since most foreigners don't have a Japanese relative to ask, you will normally use a guarantor company ({保証[ほしょう]会社[がいしゃ]}) instead. Unfortunately, some landlords still refuse foreign tenants; agencies that specialize in helping foreigners can save you time.

Layouts are written as codes: the number is the count of rooms, plus K (kitchen), DK (dining-kitchen) or LDK (living-dining-kitchen). A 1R is a single room with the kitchen in it, 1K has a separate small kitchen, and 1LDK has a bedroom plus a living area. Room sizes are often given in tatami mats ({畳[じょう]}). Contracts commonly run for two years, and in some regions renewal requires a fee ({更新料[こうしんりょう]}).

Share houses and furnished monthly apartments are an easy first step while you get your bank account, phone and job sorted out.

units.title: Garbage sorting & neighbors
units.intro:
Garbage rules in Japan are strict and set by each municipality, so the rules in your new town may differ from what a friend in another city told you. When you register at the city office or move into your building, ask for the sorting guide and collection calendar. Many cities publish them in English and other languages, and some have apps that remind you what goes out each day.

Common categories include:

- {燃[も]えるゴミ} (burnable): food waste, paper scraps, many everyday items.
- {燃[も]えないゴミ} (non-burnable): things like ceramics, small metal items, broken glass.
- {資源[しげん]ゴミ} (recyclables): cans, glass bottles, PET bottles, paper and cardboard. Usually rinsed, with caps and labels removed.
- {粗大[そだい]ゴミ} (oversized items): furniture, bicycles and so on. You normally book a collection and pay by buying a sticker or ticket.

Some cities require designated bags ({指定袋[していぶくろ]}) sold at supermarkets and convenience stores. Put garbage out on the morning of collection day, at your building's designated spot, by the time on the calendar. Wrongly sorted bags may be left behind with a warning sticker. Large appliances such as TVs, refrigerators, washing machines and air conditioners are handled under a separate recycling system and cannot go out as ordinary garbage.

Good relations with neighbors matter. Greet people you meet, keep noise down at night (walls can be thin), and follow the garbage rules; these three things prevent most problems.

If you have a noise problem with a neighbor, it is usually better to contact the management company than to confront them directly.
Ask before putting out items you are unsure about. Neighbors and building managers would much rather you ask than guess.

units.title: Post office & deliveries
units.intro:
The post office ({郵便局[ゆうびんきょく]}) handles letters, parcels, registered mail and the services of Japan Post Bank. Japanese addresses are written from largest to smallest: postal code (seven digits, after the {〒} mark), prefecture, city or ward, district, block numbers, building name and room number, then the person's name with {様[さま]}.

Private courier companies ({宅配便[たくはいびん]}) deliver most online shopping, quickly and to a chosen time slot. If you are not home, the driver leaves a missed-delivery notice ({不在[ふざい]連絡票[れんらくひょう]}) in your mailbox. It has a QR code, a website and a phone number for arranging redelivery ({再配達[さいはいたつ]}); you choose a date and time window. Many services also let you pick up at a convenience store or delivery locker, or ask for the parcel to be left at your door ({置[お]き配[はい]}).

When you move within Japan, you can submit a change-of-address notice ({転居届[てんきょとどけ]}) to the post office, and your mail is forwarded to the new address for a limited period. Note that some official mail is not forwarded, so update your address everywhere as well.

Put your name on your mailbox and door. Mail and parcels without a clearly matching name may be returned to the sender.

Be careful with text messages claiming to be from a delivery company with a link to click. Fake delivery messages are a common scam; use the official app or website instead.

If you receive a delivery text with a strange link, do not click it. Check the tracking number on the courier's official site.
Convenience stores accept parcels for several courier companies, which is handy for returns.

units.title: Making friends & social etiquette
units.intro:
Friendships in Japan often build slowly, through repeated contact in a shared setting: a hobby club ({サークル}), a sports team, a language exchange, volunteering, or regular colleagues. Showing up consistently matters more than one great conversation.

Invitations can be vague. {今度[こんど]、飲[の]みに行[い]きましょう} (let's go for a drink sometime) may be sincere or just friendly politeness. If you want to meet, follow up with a concrete day. Refusals are also indirect: {その日[ひ]はちょっと…} (that day is a bit...) is a clear no, and you shouldn't press for a reason.

Drinking parties ({飲[の]み会[かい]}) are a big part of social and work life. Wait for the toast ({乾杯[かんぱい]}) before drinking. It is polite to notice when someone's glass is empty and offer to pour. Many restaurants offer an all-you-can-drink course ({飲[の]み放題[ほうだい]}), and the bill is often split evenly ({割[わ]り勘[かん]}). You never have to drink alcohol; ordering oolong tea or a soft drink is completely normal.

Gifts are woven into daily life. After a trip, people bring souvenirs ({お土産[みやげ]}), usually individually wrapped snacks to share at work. When you visit someone's home, bring a small gift ({手土産[てみやげ]}), take your shoes off at the entrance, and say {お邪魔[じゃま]します}. If you receive a gift for a special occasion, a return gift ({お返[かえ]し}) is often expected.

With new acquaintances, start in polite speech and switch to casual speech when the other person does.

At work drinking parties, juniors often pour for seniors. If someone pours for you, lift your glass slightly with both hands.

In homes, also take off the house slippers before stepping on tatami, and use the separate toilet slippers if provided.
Switching to casual speech too early can feel pushy, and staying formal too long can feel distant. Mirror the other person.

units.title: Job hunting in Japan
units.intro:
To work in Japan you need a status of residence that allows the work you will do. At a high level, common routes are:

- **Engineer / Specialist in Humanities / International Services** ({技術[ぎじゅつ]・人文[じんぶん]知識[ちしき]・国際[こくさい]業務[ぎょうむ]}): the usual status for office, IT, engineering, translation and similar professional jobs. It generally expects a relevant degree or work experience.
- **Highly Skilled Professional** ({高度[こうど]専門職[せんもんしょく]}): a points-based status with extra benefits.
- **Specified Skilled Worker** ({特定[とくてい]技能[ぎのう]}): for certain industries with labor shortages, usually requiring skills and Japanese tests.
- Others include intra-company transfer, instructor and working holiday. Spouses of Japanese nationals and permanent residents can generally work freely, and students can work limited hours with permission.

Your employer usually provides documents for your visa application. Rules and requirements change, so always check the Immigration Services Agency.

Japanese applications usually need two documents. The {履歴書[りれきしょ]} is a resume on a standard form: personal details, photo, education and work history in date order, qualifications, and a short section on motivation. The {職務[しょくむ]経歴書[けいれきしょ]} is a freer document describing your past roles, responsibilities and achievements in detail.

Where to look: bilingual job boards, professional networking sites, recruitment agencies ({転職[てんしょく]エージェント}), which are usually free for job seekers, and Hello Work ({ハローワーク}), the public employment service. Many Japanese-speaking roles ask for JLPT N2 or N1, so list your level clearly.

tips: Use a proper ID-style photo for your {履歴書[りれきしょ]}: plain background, business clothes, recent. Photo booths at stations are made for this.

Japanese companies traditionally hire new graduates in one big yearly cycle; as a mid-career applicant you will mostly apply through {中途[ちゅうと]採用[さいよう]} postings, which open year-round.
Be clear about your visa situation early. Recruiters can match you much better when they know exactly what status you hold and when it expires.
Check whether a job is permanent ({正社員[せいしゃいん]}), contract or dispatched. Pay, job security and benefits can differ a lot.

units.title: The job interview
units.intro:
Japanese job interviews ({面接[めんせつ]}) follow a fairly set ritual, and getting the manners right makes a strong first impression. There are often several rounds, ending in a final interview with senior managers.

Arrive a few minutes early, but not too early; around five to ten minutes before is ideal. Wear a dark, conservative suit unless told otherwise. For an in-person interview, the typical sequence is:

- Knock on the door, wait for {どうぞ}, enter and say {失礼[しつれい]いたします}.
- Close the door, turn and bow, walk to the side of the chair.
- Give your name and {よろしくお願[ねが]いいたします}, and bow again.
- Sit only when invited: {どうぞおかけください}.
- At the end, stand, thank them, bow, and say {失礼[しつれい]いたします} again at the door.

Refer to the company you are applying to as {御社[おんしゃ]} when speaking (in writing it becomes {貴社[きしゃ]}), and speak in polite, humble Japanese about yourself.

Common questions include a self-introduction or self-PR, your reason for applying ({志望[しぼう]動機[どうき]}), strengths and weaknesses, why you want to work in Japan, and how long you plan to stay. At the end you will almost always be asked if you have any questions ({逆質問[ぎゃくしつもん]}); prepare at least one or two thoughtful ones. Online interviews are common too: test your camera and sound beforehand, and keep the same level of politeness.

units.title: First day at work
units.intro:
On your first day you will very likely be asked to introduce yourself to your team, often at a morning meeting ({朝礼[ちょうれい]}) or as you are walked around the office. Prepare a short speech of about 30 seconds to a minute. A common structure is:

- Your name, with the department you are joining: {本日[ほんじつ]から〜でお世話[せわ]になります}.
- Where you are from and what you did before.
- One light personal detail, if you like.
- A humble closing, asking for guidance: {ご指導[しどう]よろしくお願[ねが]いいたします}.

You will also handle paperwork: the employment contract, social insurance enrollment, a bank account for salary, your commuting route for the commuting allowance, and your My Number, which employers need for tax and social insurance. Read the work rules ({就業[しゅうぎょう]規則[きそく]}) for working hours, leave and overtime.

Learn the daily phrases. Say {おはようございます} when you arrive, {お疲[つか]れ様[さま]です} when you pass colleagues during the day, {お先[さき]に失礼[しつれい]します} when you leave before others, and {お疲[つか]れ様[さま]でした} to people who are leaving. Ask questions freely in the first weeks; it is expected of a newcomer. You will probably be assigned a mentor or senior colleague ({先輩[せんぱい]}) to help you.

Take notes, learn names and roles quickly, and watch how colleagues behave. Every workplace has its own unwritten rules.

units.title: Workplace keigo essentials
units.intro:
Keigo ({敬語[けいご]}) is the system of respectful language used at work, with customers and with anyone of higher status. It has three main layers:

- **Polite language** ({丁寧語[ていねいご]}): {です／ます}, plus {ございます} in very formal speech.
- **Respectful language** ({尊敬語[そんけいご]}): raises the other person by using special verbs for their actions, such as {いらっしゃる} (be / go / come), {おっしゃる} (say), {ご覧[らん]になる} (see), {召[め]し上[あ]がる} (eat / drink), or the pattern {お〜になる}.
- **Humble language** ({謙譲語[けんじょうご]}): lowers yourself when your action relates to the other person, such as {参[まい]る} (go / come), {申[もう]す} (say), {伺[うかが]う} (visit / ask), {拝見[はいけん]する} (see), {いただく} (receive / eat), or the pattern {お〜する}.

The key rule is **inside vs outside** ({ウチ／ソト}). Inside your company, you show respect to your boss. But when speaking to an outside person such as a client, your whole company is inside, so you talk about your boss humbly, without {さん} or a title: {部長[ぶちょう]の田中[たなか]は外出[がいしゅつ]しております}.

A few set phrases cover a huge amount of office life: {お疲[つか]れ様[さま]です}, {失礼[しつれい]します}, {かしこまりました} or {承知[しょうち]しました} (certainly / understood), {申[もう]し訳[わけ]ございません}, and cushion phrases like {恐[おそ]れ入[い]りますが} and {お手数[てすう]ですが} placed before requests.

Don't panic about perfection. Many Japanese people make keigo mistakes too. Clear polite {です／ます} with the right set phrases will carry you a long way while you learn.

Learn keigo as fixed phrases first. You will understand the system faster once you can already say the most common sentences.

units.title: Business phone etiquette
units.intro:
Many offices still expect staff, especially newer employees, to answer the phone. Business phone Japanese is highly formulaic, so once you learn the script, it becomes much less scary.

**Answering.** Pick up quickly. If it rang several times, start with {お待[ま]たせいたしました}. Then give the company name: {お電話[でんわ]ありがとうございます。株式会社[かぶしきがいしゃ]ミチでございます}. Do not say {もしもし} when answering a business call.

**Taking the caller's details.** Confirm the caller's name and company and greet them with {いつもお世話[せわ]になっております}. Repeat important details back ({復唱[ふくしょう]}), especially names, numbers and times.

**When the person is unavailable.** Explain briefly, using humble forms and no {さん} for your colleague: {あいにく田中[たなか]は席[せき]を外[はず]しております} (away from desk), {外出[がいしゅつ]しております} (out of the office), or {本日[ほんじつ]は休[やす]みをいただいております} (off today). Then offer options: a callback ({折[お]り返[かえ]し}) or taking a message ({伝言[でんごん]}).

**Leaving a note.** Write a message memo for your colleague: who called, from which company, the time, the message and the callback number, plus your name.

**Making a call.** Introduce yourself first, then ask for the person: {株式会社[かぶしきがいしゃ]ミチのスミスと申[もう]しますが、営業部[えいぎょうぶ]の鈴木[すずき]様[さま]はいらっしゃいますか}.

At the end, say {失礼[しつれい]いたします}, and wait for the other side to hang up first if they are a client or senior, then put the receiver down gently.

units.title: Business email
units.intro:
Japanese business email ({ビジネスメール}) follows a clear structure. Once you have a template, most emails are easy to write.

- **Subject** ({件名[けんめい]}): specific and informative, often with a tag in brackets, e.g. {【ご確認[かくにん]のお願[ねが]い】12月[じゅうにがつ]定例[ていれい]会議[かいぎ]の資料[しりょう]}.
- **Addressee** ({宛名[あてな]}): company, department, then name with {様[さま]}, each on its own line, e.g. {株式会社[かぶしきがいしゃ]ABC}, {営業部[えいぎょうぶ]}, {山本[やまもと]様[さま]}. Use {御中[おんちゅう]} for an organization or department without a specific person, and {各位[かくい]} for a group of people (e.g. {関係者[かんけいしゃ]各位[かくい]}).
- **Opening**: {お世話[せわ]になっております} for people outside the company, {お疲[つか]れ様[さま]です} for colleagues. Then say who you are: {株式会社[かぶしきがいしゃ]ミチのスミスです}. For a first contact, use {初[はじ]めてご連絡[れんらく]いたします}.
- **Body**: state the purpose early, keep paragraphs short and leave blank lines between them. Seasonal greetings are not needed in ordinary emails.
- **Closing**: {何卒[なにとぞ]よろしくお願[ねが]いいたします}, {引[ひ]き続[つづ]きよろしくお願[ねが]いいたします} or {ご確認[かくにん]のほど、よろしくお願[ねが]いいたします}.
- **Signature** ({署名[しょめい]}): name, company, department, phone and email.

When replying, keep the original subject line so the thread stays together. If you are late, start with an apology for the delay. Many companies now use chat tools for internal communication, which are lighter in tone, but emails to clients remain formal.

units.title: Meetings & reporting (hōrensō)
units.intro:
One of the first workplace concepts you will hear about is {報連相[ほうれんそう]} (hōrensō), a pun on the word for spinach. It stands for three habits that Japanese managers value highly:

- {報告[ほうこく]} (report): tell your boss about progress and results, without waiting to be asked. Report bad news, such as delays and mistakes, early.
- {連絡[れんらく]} (inform): share facts, such as schedule changes and absences, with everyone affected.
- {相談[そうだん]} (consult): ask for advice before making a decision or when you are stuck, rather than deciding alone.

When reporting, start with the conclusion ({結論[けつろん]から申[もう]しますと}), then the reason, then what you propose.

Meetings range from formal {会議[かいぎ]} to smaller working sessions ({打[う]ち合[あ]わせ}). In many Japanese organizations, important decisions are prepared before the meeting through informal consultation with key people ({根回[ねまわ]し}), so the meeting itself often confirms what was already discussed. If you want to propose something, talk to the right people beforehand.

Junior members are often asked to take minutes ({議事録[ぎじろく]}). When you disagree, soften it: acknowledge the other view first ({おっしゃることはよくわかります}), then give yours ({ただ、〜}). A phrase you will hear from clients is {持[も]ち帰[かえ]って検討[けんとう]いたします} (we'll take this back and consider it), which means no decision today. Written approval flows ({稟議[りんぎ]}) are also common for spending and new projects.

units.title: Business cards & hierarchy
units.intro:
Exchanging business cards ({名刺[めいし]交換[こうかん]}) is a small ritual at first meetings with people from other companies. A card represents its owner, so handle it with care.

- Keep cards in a card case ({名刺入[めいしい]れ}), not loose in a pocket or wallet.
- Stand up and face the other person, ideally without a table between you.
- The visitor, or the more junior person, usually offers first.
- Hold your card with both hands, turned so the other person can read it, and say your company and name: {株式会社[かぶしきがいしゃ]ミチのスミスと申[もう]します}.
- Hold your card slightly lower than theirs as a sign of humility.
- If you exchange at the same time, give with your right hand and receive with your left, then support it with both hands.
- Receive with {頂戴[ちょうだい]いたします}, and take a moment to look at the name and title.

During the meeting, lay the cards on the table in front of you in the order people are seated. The most senior person's card is often placed on top of your card case. Never write on someone's card in front of them, and put the cards away carefully at the end.

Hierarchy shows up everywhere. Common titles include {社長[しゃちょう]} (president), {部長[ぶちょう]} (department head), {課長[かちょう]} (section head) and {係長[かかりちょう]} (group leader), though titles vary by company. Seating also follows rank: the place of honor ({上座[かみざ]}) is usually farthest from the door, and the lowest seat ({下座[しもざ]}) is nearest the door. Guests and seniors get the {上座[かみざ]}.

units.title: Asking for time off & sick days
units.intro:
Japanese law gives employees paid annual leave ({年次[ねんじ]有給[ゆうきゅう]休暇[きゅうか]}, usually just {有給[ゆうきゅう]}). In broad terms, after about six months of continuous employment with good attendance, full-time workers receive an initial allowance of days, which increases with years of service, and employers must make sure that workers with a sufficient allowance actually take a minimum number of days each year. Unused days can be carried over for a limited time. The exact numbers depend on your situation and company, so check your contract, your company's work rules ({就業[しゅうぎょう]規則[きそく]}) and official labor guidance.

In practice, ask for leave well in advance, follow your company's request system, and coordinate with your team so your work is covered. You generally don't need to give a detailed reason; {私用[しよう]のため} (for personal reasons) is the standard phrase.

There is no general legal requirement for separate paid sick leave, so many people use {有給[ゆうきゅう]} days when they are ill; some companies offer their own sick leave. If you are off work for a long illness, employee health insurance may pay a partial income allowance ({傷病[しょうびょう]手当金[てあてきん]}) after a waiting period.

When you are sick, contact your boss before your start time, by phone or by the method your team uses. Keep it short: what is wrong, that you will rest, and how urgent work is being handled. Major holiday periods are Golden Week in spring, Obon in August and the New Year holidays, when trains and flights are very busy.

units.title: Taxes & payslips
units.intro:
Your payslip ({給与[きゅうよ]明細[めいさい]}) has two main parts. **Payments** ({支給[しきゅう]}) include base salary ({基本給[きほんきゅう]}), overtime pay and allowances such as the commuting allowance. **Deductions** ({控除[こうじょ]}) usually include health insurance, employee pension ({厚生[こうせい]年金[ねんきん]}), employment insurance ({雇用[こよう]保険[ほけん]}), income tax ({所得税[しょとくぜい]}) and resident tax ({住民税[じゅうみんぜい]}). What actually reaches your bank account is your take-home pay ({手取[てど]り}).

**Income tax** is withheld from each paycheck ({源泉[げんせん]徴収[ちょうしゅう]}). Near the end of the year, your employer settles the exact amount in a year-end adjustment ({年末[ねんまつ]調整[ちょうせい]}), for which you submit forms about dependents and certain insurance. Afterward you receive a withholding slip ({源泉[げんせん]徴収票[ちょうしゅうひょう]}). Keep it; you will need it for many things.

**Resident tax** is a local tax calculated on your previous year's income, based mainly on where you lived at the start of the year. For employees it is usually deducted from salary over twelve months starting around June. This is why many newcomers pay little or none in their first months and then see it appear later.

**Final tax return** ({確定[かくてい]申告[しんこく]}): most salaried employees with one employer don't need to file, because the year-end adjustment handles it. You may need or want to file if you are self-employed, have significant side income, work for more than one employer, or want to claim deductions such as high medical costs. The filing period is roughly mid-February to mid-March, and online filing is available.

Tax rules are detailed and change; confirm with the National Tax Agency, your tax office or your city office.

tips: Keep every {源泉[げんせん]徴収票[ちょうしゅうひょう]}. They are needed for tax returns, loans, and sometimes visa procedures.
Visa renewals and permanent residency applications often ask for proof that your taxes and social insurance are paid. Paying on time protects your status.
If you leave a job mid-year, remaining resident tax may be taken from your last salary or billed to you directly. Watch your mail.
If you leave Japan with taxes still to pay, you may need to settle them before leaving or appoint a tax representative. Ask your city office and tax office.
Japan's hometown tax donation scheme ({ふるさと納税[のうぜい]}) can reduce your tax in exchange for donations to municipalities; read the official rules and limits before using it.

units.title: Changing jobs & resigning
units.intro:
Changing jobs ({転職[てんしょく]}) is now common in Japan, but leaving well still matters.

**Telling your company.** Speak to your direct boss first, in private and in person, before telling colleagues. Check your work rules for the required notice period; companies commonly ask for one month or more. Following your company's process makes for a smoother exit ({円満[えんまん]退職[たいしょく]}). You may be asked to submit a written resignation. A {退職願[たいしょくねがい]} is a request to resign, while a {退職届[たいしょくとどけ]} is a formal notice; many companies have their own form. The standard reason written is {一身上[いっしんじょう]の都合[つごう]により} (for personal reasons).

**Before you leave.** Prepare a handover ({引[ひ]き継[つ]ぎ}), agree on your last working day, and plan any remaining paid leave. Return your ID card, health insurance card if you have one, and company equipment. Ask for the documents you will need: the withholding slip, your pension details, and, if you may claim unemployment benefits, the separation notice ({離職票[りしょくひょう]}).

**Visa and insurance.** If your status of residence is tied to your work, there are usually notification duties to the Immigration Services Agency when you leave or join an employer, with a short deadline. Long periods without the activity your status covers can also cause problems. Your health insurance and pension change when you leave a company, so arrange the switch promptly. Confirm the details with the Immigration Services Agency and your city office.

Tell your boss before anyone else at work. Your boss hearing it from a colleague first can damage the relationship.
Look up the Immigration Services Agency's notification for changes of employer as soon as your dates are fixed; it can usually be done online.
Ask HR in writing for the documents you need after leaving and when they will be sent. Some, like the withholding slip, may arrive weeks later.
A short farewell email ({退職[たいしょく]のご挨拶[あいさつ]}) to colleagues and key clients on your last day is standard; include who will take over your work.
